newsitem.title: USA: Fla.judge weighs gag order in tobacco class action.
newsitem.headline: Fla.judge weighs gag order in tobacco class action.

text.p: A Florida judge on Monday said he would consider an industry request for gag order relating to an upcoming class-action lawsuit against the tobacco industry, and he cautioned attorneys for both sides about their public discussion of the case.

"I don't want a prejudiced jury," said Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye. He said he wanted to give both sides a "word of caution," saying, "if you really want a fair jury, you are going to have to be circumspect in the things you say and do."

Philip Morris Cos Inc on Friday asked the court to impose a gag order on Stanley Rosenblatt, who represents thousands of flight attendants in a class-action suit against the tobacco industry alleging that second-hand cigarette smoke made them ill.

"Mr. Rosenblatt has been regularly utilizing the media, we believe, to prejudice members of the public, including potential Dade County jurors," said Philip Morris attorney David Hardy during a pretrial hearing.
"We're asking the court to muzzle Mr. Rosenblatt from discussing the merits of the litigation this close to trial," he said.
The trial, the first ever of a class-action lawsuit against cigarette makers, is due to begin on June 2.
Hardy said Rosenblatt acted improperly by leaking to the Miami Herarld the transcript of videotaped depositions taken from tobacco industry chief executives.
Rosenblatt also showed excerpts from those depositions on the CBS television show "60 Minutes" on Sunday night.

Rosenblatt contended that media interest in the tobacco industry was extremely intense having nothing to do with his involvement. "The concept of drumming up publicity on this case is absurd on its face," he said.

Attorneys for three newspapers -- the Wall Street Journal, Miami Herald and USA Today -- asked the court not to impose the gag order. "It would be a complete violation of the First Amendment to the Constitution," Dan Paul, attorney for Dow Jones & Co, which owns the Journal, told the court.

Attorneys later argued over the proposed plan for the trial. The tobacco industry wants the jury initially to consider whether second-hand smoke causes disease and later the industry's liability. The plaintiffs do not want the two issues separated.
